mcq.stem: In ASP.NET Core MVC, what is the Controller's primary responsibility when an HTTP request is routed to one of its action methods?
options: Contain the HTML markup and Razor syntax that produces the final page
Handle the request, coordinate with the Model to get data, and select a View to render the response
Represent the application's data and enforce its business rules and validation
Compile Razor templates into C# classes and stream HTML to the client
mcq.explanation: The Controller handles user interaction: it processes the request, works with the Model, and picks a View to render. Holding markup and Razor is the View's job. Representing data and business rules is the Model's job. Compiling Razor templates is the view engine's responsibility, not the Controller's.

mcq.stem: How does ASP.NET Core MVC model binding populate a controller action's parameters from an incoming request?
options: It deserializes the entire raw HTTP request body into a single dynamic object
It only reads values from the query string; form and route data must be parsed manually
It matches request values to parameter names, searching sources such as form data, route values, and query string
It requires every parameter to be annotated with a [FromX] attribute or binding fails
mcq.explanation: Model binding inspects the action's parameters and looks for matching values across several request sources in a defined order, typically form data, then route values, then query string. It does not need explicit [FromX] attributes for common cases, reads more than the query string, and produces typed parameters rather than one dynamic blob.

mcq.stem: Why do ASP.NET Core controller actions typically return IActionResult rather than a raw domain object?
options: Raw objects cannot be serialized to JSON by the framework
IActionResult automatically wraps every return value in a 500 error for safety
It bypasses the response pipeline and writes directly to the socket
It lets a single action return different HTTP responses (200, 404, 302, and so on) depending on execution flow
mcq.explanation: IActionResult is an abstraction the framework executes to build the final HTTP response, so one action can conditionally return a view, a 404, a redirect, and more. The framework serializes raw objects fine, IActionResult does not force errors, and it defers response writing to the framework rather than writing to the socket directly.

mcq.stem: What happens to conventional routing for a controller once you place a [Route] attribute on that controller class?
options: Conventional routing is ignored for that controller; it relies entirely on attribute routing
Both apply, and the framework picks whichever produces the shorter URL
Conventional routing still applies, and the attribute merely adds an alias
The controller becomes unreachable until MapControllerRoute is removed
mcq.explanation: Attribute and conventional routing can coexist in an application, but once a controller carries a [Route] attribute it is opted out of conventional routing entirely and must be reached via its attribute routes. The framework does not blend the two per controller or treat the attribute as an alias.

mcq.stem: What is the main advantage of Tag Helpers (for example asp-action) over HTML Helpers (for example @Html.ActionLink) in Razor views?
options: Tag Helpers execute on the client, reducing server load
Tag Helpers are the only way to generate URLs from the routing engine
HTML Helpers cannot access the model, but Tag Helpers can
Tag Helpers produce HTML-like markup that is easier to read and style and gets better editor tooling
mcq.explanation: Tag Helpers attach to HTML-like elements and attributes, so markup stays readable to front-end developers and benefits from IntelliSense. Both run server-side, both can use routing and the model, and HTML Helpers can also generate routed URLs.

mcq.stem: After server-side validation fails on a POST, a redisplayed form shows all fields blank. What is the correct fix?
options: Call ModelState.Clear() before returning the view
Redirect to the GET action so the form reloads fresh
Pass the same model instance that was just bound back into View(model)
Replace the model with a new, empty instance before returning the view
mcq.explanation: Razor repopulates the input fields from the posted values held on the model, so the action must return View(model) with the exact object that was bound. Returning View() or a new empty instance gives Razor nothing to render, blanking the fields, and clearing ModelState or redirecting also discards the user's input.

mcq.stem: A controller action is slow because it must fetch products, call a weather API, and check permissions to build one page. How do View Components help?
options: They cache the entire rendered page so subsequent requests skip all three calls
They let each independent UI section own its own logic and data-fetching in a reusable mini-controller
They move the weather and permission calls onto the client as JavaScript
They run the controller action on a background thread pool
mcq.explanation: A View Component is a self-contained unit with its own InvokeAsync that fetches its own data and renders its own markup, so the main controller stops doing unrelated work and the widget can be reused elsewhere. They are not a page cache, do not move logic to the client, and do not simply re-thread the action.

mcq.stem: An attacker floods a costly [HttpPost] registration endpoint, overwhelming the database. Which defense most directly stops the load before it reaches the controller and database?
options: Adding [ValidateAntiForgeryToken] so unauthenticated requests are rejected
Moving password hashing to a background queue
Rate limiting middleware that returns 429 for excess requests per IP before MVC runs
Adding more Data Annotation validation to the registration view model
mcq.explanation: Rate limiting middleware sits early in the pipeline and rejects requests over the configured threshold with 429 before the action, hashing, or database inserts execute. Anti-forgery and CAPTCHA add friction but are secondary, model validation still runs the expensive pipeline, and backgrounding the hash does not cap request volume.

mcq.stem: In Razor, what does the @ symbol do when you write @Model.Name inside a .cshtml file?
options: It injects a C# expression's value into the HTML, HTML-encoded by default
It emits the literal text Model.Name into the output
It performs an unescaped string substitution with no encoding
It marks a client-side template placeholder resolved by JavaScript
mcq.explanation: A single @ followed by an expression writes that C# value into the output, and Razor HTML-encodes it by default to help prevent XSS. It is real compiled C#, not literal text or a client-side placeholder, and encoding is applied unless you explicitly opt out with Html.Raw.

mcq.stem: What is the key difference between a Partial View and a View Component in ASP.NET Core MVC?
options: A Partial View can inject services; a View Component cannot
A View Component renders without a layout, while a Partial View always includes one
They are identical; View Component is just the newer name for a Partial View
A Partial View renders markup from a model the parent supplies; a View Component can fetch its own data via its own logic
mcq.explanation: A Partial View is pure markup reuse and depends on the parent view to hand it a model. A View Component has its own InvokeAsync that can call services or a database independently. Neither is merely a rename, and layout behavior is not the distinguishing factor.

mcq.stem: When are ASP.NET Core MVC Areas an appropriate choice?
options: In almost any app, since they are the standard way to organize controllers and views
Only when an app has multiple large, clearly distinct functional zones such as a storefront, an admin back-office, and a blog
Whenever a controller has more than five action methods
Only in APIs, to group endpoints by version
mcq.explanation: Areas partition a large application into mini-applications with their own controllers and views and are worth their friction only when there are genuinely separate functional zones. For small or medium apps, plain folder organization is usually enough, and action count or API versioning is not the trigger.

mcq.stem: What does the asp-for Tag Helper on an input such as asp-for="Email" generate automatically?
options: Only a name attribute; id and value must still be written by hand
Client-side JavaScript that submits the field via AJAX
A database column mapping for the property
The name, id, current value, and an appropriate type, all derived from the model property
mcq.explanation: asp-for inspects the bound model property and emits the matching name, id, current value, and even a suitable type such as type of email. It also ties the markup to the C# property so a rename breaks the build. It does not wire up AJAX or database mappings.

mcq.stem: When is a custom IModelBinder genuinely warranted instead of the default model binder?
options: Whenever an action takes more than three parameters
For every action that accepts a POST body, for performance
When request data's shape does not map onto the default name-matching convention, for example ids=1,2,3 becoming a List of int
Only when binding primitive types like int or bool
mcq.explanation: The default binder already handles primitives, DTOs, nested objects, and collections via name matching. A custom binder is for shapes it has no rule for, such as a single comma-separated value that must become a list, or combining several parameters into one value object. It is not needed for parameter count, POST bodies in general, or primitives.

mcq.stem: Why does ASP.NET Core's response compression default EnableForHttps to false?
options: Compression over TLS is computationally impossible without hardware support
Browsers reject gzip or Brotli responses served over HTTPS
Compressing a response that mixes attacker-influenced input with secrets can leak the secret via observable response size (BREACH/CRIME style attacks)
HTTPS already compresses payloads, so a second pass corrupts them
mcq.explanation: When a compressed response body contains both attacker-controlled reflected text and a secret, an attacker who can observe response size can watch it shrink as guesses match and extract the secret incrementally. That risk is why HTTPS compression is opt-in. TLS does not compress, browsers accept compressed responses, and compression over TLS is entirely feasible.

mcq.stem: How does a PartialViewResult differ from a ViewResult returned by a controller action?
options: PartialViewResult renders an HTML fragment without the shared _Layout wrapper
PartialViewResult returns JSON instead of HTML
PartialViewResult can only be returned from API controllers
PartialViewResult always triggers a client-side redirect
mcq.explanation: PartialView renders just the view fragment with no _Layout wrapper, which suits AJAX updates to part of an already-loaded page. ViewResult renders a full page inside the layout. Both return HTML, both work in MVC controllers, and neither redirects.

mcq.stem: What does implementing IValidatableObject on a model let you express that individual Data Annotation attributes cannot?
options: Asynchronous validation that awaits external services
Client-side validation without any JavaScript
Validation that runs only when explicitly called from the controller
Validation rules that depend on the relationship between two or more properties
mcq.explanation: Data Annotations validate one property in isolation, so a rule like end date must be after start date needs IValidatableObject's Validate method, which the framework calls automatically as part of the normal ModelState.IsValid check. It is not an async mechanism, does not provide client-side validation on its own, and does not require manual invocation.

mcq.stem: Why must UseAuthorization() be placed after UseRouting() but before endpoint execution (MapControllers)?
options: UseRouting resets the HttpContext, which authorization needs freshly initialized
Routing matches the endpoint first, so authorization middleware can read the matched endpoint's [Authorize] metadata before the action runs
Authorization can only read cookies after routing has parsed the URL
It is a naming convention with no functional effect on ordering
mcq.explanation: Endpoint routing splits matching from execution: UseRouting resolves which endpoint will handle the request, so middleware after it can call GetEndpoint() and inspect metadata like [Authorize] policies, then enforce them before the endpoint executes. Placed before UseRouting, no endpoint is matched yet and GetEndpoint() returns null.

mcq.stem: What is the purpose of the _ViewStart.cshtml file?
options: It defines the shared HTML structure such as header and footer that wraps every view
It runs code (commonly setting Layout) before each view in its folder and subfolders, so the assignment is not repeated per view
It registers Tag Helpers and namespace imports for all views
It is the first view rendered when the application starts
mcq.explanation: Razor executes _ViewStart.cshtml before rendering each regular view in the same folder tree, most often to set Layout once. The layout markup itself lives in _Layout.cshtml, Tag Helper and using imports go in _ViewImports.cshtml, and it is not an application entry point.

mcq.stem: Why is generating a URL with Url.Action("Details", "Products", new { id = 5 }) preferable to writing the string "/Products/Details/5" by hand?
options: Url.Action produces shorter URLs than hardcoded strings
Hardcoded strings are blocked by the framework at runtime
Url.Action encrypts the URL to prevent tampering
Url.Action builds the URL from the current routing configuration, so it stays correct if routes change
mcq.explanation: Url.Action asks the routing system to construct the URL from the routes actually registered, so a later change to route templates is reflected automatically everywhere it is called. A hand-typed string has no link to the routing table and silently goes stale. It is not about length, encryption, or a runtime ban on literals.

mcq.stem: What does a custom IRouteConstraint let you do that built-in constraints like {id:int} do not?
options: Return a detailed 400 Bad Request describing why a route value was rejected
Bind the route value to a custom .NET type
Apply arbitrary, domain-specific logic to decide whether a URL segment matches the route at all
Cache the matched route for subsequent requests
mcq.explanation: A custom route constraint runs your own Match logic, for example a SKU format check, to decide if the route matches; a non-matching value simply makes the route fail and routing falls through, typically to a 404, with no validation message. For client-facing error detail you would validate inside the action instead. It does not do type binding or caching.

mcq.stem: What is the relationship between ViewBag and ViewData in ASP.NET Core MVC?
options: ViewBag is a dynamic wrapper over the same underlying ViewData dictionary
ViewBag is stored in session; ViewData is per-request
ViewBag is strongly typed; ViewData is not
They are completely separate stores that must be kept in sync manually
mcq.explanation: ViewBag is just a dynamic-typed syntax over the identical ViewData dictionary, so ViewBag.Title and ViewData indexed by Title refer to the same value. Both are per-request and resolved at runtime with no compile-time checking, which is why a strongly-typed model is preferred for a view's primary data.

mcq.stem: A recent-orders widget appears on several pages and needs its own database query. Why is a View Component a better fit than a Partial View?
options: A Partial View cannot render inside a layout, but a View Component can
View Components render faster because they skip Razor compilation
A Partial View cannot accept a model from its parent
The View Component fetches its own data, so each hosting controller action does not have to load and pass it
mcq.explanation: Because a View Component's InvokeAsync injects services and fetches its own data, the widget can be dropped onto any page without that page's action knowing it exists. A Partial-View approach would force every hosting action to run and pass the widget's query. Partials do accept a parent model and do render within layouts, and compilation is not the difference.

mcq.stem: What does an IApplicationModelConvention let you do at application startup?
options: Intercept each HTTP request and rewrite its route values
Programmatically apply a cross-cutting rule such as a route prefix or filter to many controllers and actions at once, without touching their code
Replace the JSON serializer used for all responses
Cache controller instances between requests
mcq.explanation: Conventions run once during startup over MVC's ApplicationModel of all discovered controllers and actions and let you mutate it in bulk, for example adding a route prefix to every controller in a namespace. It is not a per-request hook, not a serializer setting, and not about instance caching.

mcq.stem: How does the [Bind] attribute help protect against mass assignment / over-posting?
options: It encrypts form fields so they cannot be tampered with in transit
It rejects the entire request if any unexpected field is present
It marks the model as read-only after binding
It restricts model binding to an explicit whitelist of properties, ignoring any other fields in the request
mcq.explanation: [Bind] limits binding to the named properties, so an attacker-supplied extra field such as isAdmin=true is simply not populated. It does not encrypt anything, does not reject the request, and does not freeze the object. A purpose-built request DTO that lacks the sensitive property is the more robust modern approach.

mcq.stem: How does the <vc:recent-orders> Tag Helper syntax relate to @await Component.InvokeAsync("RecentOrders", ...)?
options: The Tag Helper form runs the component on the client; the InvokeAsync form runs it on the server
The Tag Helper form skips the component's InvokeAsync method entirely
They invoke the same View Component; the Tag Helper form is a declarative HTML-like alternative with attributes as parameters
The Tag Helper form caches the component output; the InvokeAsync form does not
mcq.explanation: Both syntaxes call the same view component's InvokeAsync; the tag form just reads more like HTML, mapping kebab-case attributes such as customer-id to parameters such as customerId, and requires the view component Tag Helper to be registered in _ViewImports.cshtml. Neither runs on the client or changes caching.

mcq.stem: How does IApiDescriptionProvider support automatic Swagger/OpenAPI generation?
options: It builds a machine-readable description of each action's route, verb, parameters, and response types that tooling consumes
It serves a static OpenAPI YAML file bundled with the app
It proxies requests to an external documentation service
It rewrites controller code at build time to match a hand-authored spec
mcq.explanation: MVC uses IApiDescriptionProvider to describe every action from its route template, HTTP verb, parameters, and ProducesResponseType annotations, and tools like Swashbuckle or NSwag query that description to emit an always-current OpenAPI document. There is no bundled static file, external proxy, or code rewriting involved.

mcq.stem: Why would an action call ModelState.AddModelError(...) instead of returning a custom error object?
options: It logs the error to the configured logging provider automatically
It halts the request pipeline immediately
It converts the error into an unhandled exception
It reports a business-rule violation through the same ModelState mechanism and response shape as Data Annotation failures
mcq.explanation: AddModelError puts a custom error into the same ModelState structure the Data Annotations populate, so BadRequest(ModelState) returns one consistent validation-error shape whether the failure was declarative or a manual business check. It does not auto-log, short-circuit the pipeline, or throw.

mcq.stem: What does the VaryByQueryKeys parameter of [ResponseCache] do?
options: It excludes the listed query parameters from the cache key
It causes responses to be cached and served separately for each distinct combination of the listed query parameter values
It limits caching to requests that omit those query parameters
It encrypts the listed query parameters in the cached copy
mcq.explanation: VaryByQueryKeys tells the cache to key entries by the values of the named query parameters, so category=books&page=1 and category=books&page=2 get separate cached responses. Without it, a cache could serve one combination's response to a request with different parameters, which is a correctness bug.

mcq.stem: What does implementing IAuthorizationMiddlewareResultHandler allow an application to customize?
options: Which authorization policies are registered at startup
How claims are extracted from an incoming JWT
The response produced when an authorization check fails, for example a structured JSON body instead of a bare 403
The order in which authorization and routing middleware run
mcq.explanation: The handler intercepts the authorization middleware's outcome, letting you replace the default bare 401/403 with custom logic like a JSON error body or a redirect. Typically you override only the failure case and delegate the success path to the default handler. It does not define policies, parse tokens, or reorder middleware.

mcq.stem: Why is returning PartialView() well suited to an endpoint consumed by AJAX for a partial page update?
options: It returns only an HTML fragment with no full-document or layout wrapper, ready to insert into the DOM
It automatically converts the response to JSON for fetch()
It forces the browser to perform a full navigation
It compresses the response more aggressively than View()
mcq.explanation: PartialView renders just the fragment's markup without the html, head, or _Layout wrapper, so client-side JavaScript can drop it straight into an existing page. Returning a full View would send an entire redundant document. It does not emit JSON, navigate, or change compression.

mcq.stem: A model must enforce that EndDate is not earlier than StartDate. Which mechanism fits, and why not a plain Data Annotation?
options: A [Range] attribute on EndDate referencing StartDate
A custom middleware that inspects the request body
Client-side JavaScript only, since dates are a UI concern
IValidatableObject.Validate, because the rule spans two properties and integrates with the same ModelState check
mcq.explanation: Data Annotations validate a single property in isolation, so a two-property relationship needs IValidatableObject's Validate method, whose results feed the same ModelState.IsValid check as Required or Range. Range cannot reference another property, and middleware or client-only checks are not the model-level validation mechanism.

mcq.stem: What problem does a custom IActionConstraint solve?
options: Validating the format of a single URL segment like {id}
Restricting an action to authenticated users
Choosing between multiple actions that share the identical route template and HTTP verb, based on a runtime condition
Serializing an action's result to a custom format
mcq.explanation: IActionConstraint's Accept method lets routing pick between actions that would otherwise both match the same route and verb, using conditions like the presence of a specific header. Segment-shape validation is a route constraint's job, auth is handled by Authorize, and serialization is an output formatter's job.

mcq.stem: How do Data Annotations like [Required] and [StringLength] get enforced in MVC?
options: The developer must call model.Validate() at the start of each action
The model binder checks them against incoming data and populates ModelState before the action body executes
They are enforced only by client-side JavaScript
They generate database CHECK constraints at migration time
mcq.explanation: During model binding the framework evaluates the annotations and records any violations in ModelState, so the action just checks ModelState.IsValid. They also drive client-side validation via Tag Helpers, but enforcement is automatic server-side and unrelated to database schema.

mcq.stem: In MVC's filter pipeline, which filter type wraps execution of the IActionResult itself, for example rendering the view or serializing JSON?
options: IActionFilter
IExceptionFilter
IResultFilter
IAuthorizationFilter
mcq.explanation: IResultFilter's OnResultExecuting and OnResultExecuted run around the result writing the HTTP response, which is where you would inspect or modify the rendered output. IActionFilter wraps only the action method call, IExceptionFilter runs when something throws, and IAuthorizationFilter runs first, before the action.

mcq.stem: How do you make [ValidateAntiForgeryToken] work for a fetch()-based POST that sends JSON rather than an HTML form?
options: Disable anti-forgery for the endpoint since JSON requests are immune to CSRF
Put the token in the URL query string
Rely on the browser to attach the token cookie automatically
Read the token from the page and send it in a custom header, with the antiforgery service configured to accept that header
mcq.explanation: A fetch request submits no hidden form field, so you retrieve the rendered token and attach it as a header, and configure AddAntiforgery to read that header name. Cookie-authenticated JSON endpoints are still CSRF-vulnerable, so disabling protection is wrong, and the query string or automatic cookie behavior do not satisfy the validation.

mcq.stem: Why does MVC convention favor a purpose-built ViewModel per view over passing a domain entity to Razor?
options: Domain entities cannot be serialized by the Razor engine
A ViewModel carries exactly what the view needs, possibly from multiple sources plus UI-only fields, and decouples the view from entity and schema changes
ViewModels render faster because they have fewer properties
Razor requires every model to implement an IViewModel interface
mcq.explanation: A ViewModel is shaped for one view: it can combine data from several entities, add formatted or UI-only values, and insulate the view from database or entity changes, while avoiding accidentally exposing sensitive fields. It is not a serialization limitation, a performance trick, or an interface requirement.

mcq.stem: How does MVC's client-side (unobtrusive) validation avoid duplicating validation logic in hand-written JavaScript?
options: It sends every keystroke to the server for validation
Tag Helpers emit data-val attributes from the model's Data Annotations, which a bundled jQuery library reads to validate in the browser
It compiles the C# validation attributes to WebAssembly
It disables server-side validation once the client library loads
mcq.explanation: The same Required or EmailAddress attributes that drive server-side ModelState also generate data-val attributes via Tag Helpers, and jquery.validate.unobtrusive.js enforces them client-side, so the rule is defined once. Server-side validation must still run because any non-browser client bypasses the JavaScript.

mcq.stem: What does writing a Custom Tag Helper give you over repeating raw markup or a C# helper method in each view?
options: Client-side rendering of the markup for better performance
Automatic database persistence of the rendered element
The ability to bypass Razor's HTML encoding globally
Reusable server-side HTML-generation logic behind HTML-like syntax that integrates with Razor IntelliSense
mcq.explanation: A Custom Tag Helper centralizes rendering logic, for example status-to-CSS-class mapping, in one Process method and exposes it as an HTML-like tag with strongly-typed attributes and IntelliSense, unlike a Partial View call or a C# helper returning an HTML string. It still runs server-side and does not touch persistence or global encoding.

mcq.stem: When an action calls return View() with no view name, where does MVC look for the .cshtml file?
options: Only in a flat /Views folder, matched by the model's type name
In the same folder as the controller's .cs file
First Views/{ControllerName}/{ActionName}.cshtml, then Views/Shared/{ActionName}.cshtml
Wherever a [ViewLocation] attribute on the action points
mcq.explanation: The default convention derives the path from the executing controller and action, checking the controller-specific folder first and then Views/Shared, using the first match. It is not based on model type, the controller's source location, or a required attribute.

mcq.stem: How does the default model binder reconstruct a List property on a view model from posted form data?
options: It requires the list to be posted as a single JSON string
It groups fields named with the indexed convention such as Items[0].Name and Items[1].Name into distinct collection elements
It binds list items in whatever order the fields appear, ignoring names
It only supports collections of primitives, not complex types
mcq.explanation: The binder relies on square-bracket index names to know which flat fields belong to which element, expecting sequential zero-based indices. asp-for inside a for loop generates these automatically. It handles complex element types and does not need a JSON blob.

mcq.stem: How does a custom IModelBinderProvider differ from directly implementing IModelBinder?
options: The provider inspects the type being bound and decides which binder, if any, handles it, returning null to defer to others
The provider runs on every request; the binder runs only at startup
The provider validates the bound value; the binder only reads it
They are interchangeable; either can be registered the same way
mcq.explanation: An IModelBinder holds logic for one scenario; an IModelBinderProvider sits above it, examining the model type and returning a binder for types it wants to handle or null to fall through to the next provider and the framework defaults. That is what lets a custom binder apply only to its intended type.

mcq.stem: What does a Razor @section (with @RenderSection in the layout) let a child view do?
options: Override the layout's Layout property for that view
Replace the entire layout with a different one
Share C# variables between unrelated views
Inject content into a named placeholder the layout defines, such as a page-specific scripts block
mcq.explanation: The layout declares named sections with RenderSection, and a child view supplies matching content with an @section block that renders at that spot. Marking a section as not required lets views omit it. It does not swap layouts or share variables across views.

mcq.stem: Why did the ASP.NET Core ecosystem shift from HtmlHelper extension methods toward Tag Helpers for reusable HTML generation?
options: HtmlHelper methods could not access dependency injection
Tag Helpers' HTML-like syntax blends into markup-heavy views and integrates with editor tooling, unlike C#-method-call syntax
HtmlHelper methods were removed from ASP.NET Core
Tag Helpers execute client-side, reducing server work
mcq.explanation: @Html.X() method calls stand out awkwardly in otherwise HTML markup, while Tag Helpers look like elements and attributes and get IntelliSense. HtmlHelper still exists and works, both run server-side, and DI access was not the deciding factor.

mcq.stem: How does [ModelBinder(BinderType = typeof(X))] on an action parameter differ from registering a global IModelBinderProvider for that type?
options: The attribute applies the binder to every parameter of that type in the app
The attribute runs the binder at startup instead of per request
The attribute applies the binder only to that one parameter, leaving other parameters of the same type on the default binder
There is no difference; both are application-wide
mcq.explanation: The attribute is narrowly scoped to the single decorated parameter, so the same type bound elsewhere keeps default behavior. A global provider forces the custom binder onto every occurrence of the type, which can cause unintended side effects on unrelated parameters.

mcq.stem: What is TempData used for that ViewData/ViewBag cannot handle?
options: Passing large primary datasets to a view with compile-time safety
Storing data for the entire lifetime of the user's session
Sharing data between concurrent requests from different users
Persisting a value across a single redirect, after which it is automatically cleared
mcq.explanation: TempData is stored in a cookie or session so it survives one redirect, the Post-Redirect-Get case, and is then removed. ViewData and ViewBag live only for the current request. Session state covers longer-lived per-user data, and none of these share data across users.
